title: What Did Pirates Do When They Weren’t Raiding Ships?
alternate_titles: A Pirate’s Day Off Was Still Hard Work
period: Early 1718, aboard a reconstruction of Queen Anne's Revenge off the southeastern coast of North America, before her June grounding. Low timber working decks, hemp rope, wooden blocks, plain canvas sails, wooden barrels and plain clothing: linen shirts, waistcoats, breeches, caps and soft felt hats. No claim to an archaeologically certain deck plan. The same modest working space and adult crew recur. Modern archaeological explanations use neutral parchment; the clearly labelled Roberts comparison belongs to another crew in 1719–1722.
avoid: Hollywood pirate uniforms, skulls on every object, treasure islands, parrots, eye patches on all sailors, theatrical long coats on working crew, modern tattoos, oversized galleon castles, steam, steel modern railings, electric light, ship's wheel without a verified reference, modern surgical instruments, bloody procedures, literal treasure heaps, invented readable charts, book titles drawn by the image model, background Visitor, treating enslaved or coerced people as cheerful volunteers.

deck.scope: Queen Anne's Revenge, early 1718; illustrative working deck
deck.design: Timber bulwark left with sea beyond, one mast base rear-left, a neatly secured rope coil at left, clear level deck on right. No wheel, flags, guns firing or exact unsupported vessel silhouette. Adult sailor A: brown waistcoat, cream shirt, slate breeches, plain brown cap.

galley.scope: Queen Anne's Revenge, early 1718; illustrative food preparation space
galley.design: A small contained brick-lined cooking hearth at far left, iron pot firmly supported, plain chopping board and covered wooden barrel. Safe separation from canvas and loose rope. One adult cook in cream shirt, brown breeches, no costume accessories; do not claim portrait identity.

food.scope: Material found at the Queen Anne's Revenge wreck; explanatory reconstruction
food.design: Neutral parchment field, simplified butchered cattle or pig bone and plain bowl as specified. No specimen identification labels painted; show reconstructed whole object, not invented exact museum artifact.

repair.scope: Queen Anne's Revenge, early 1718; illustrative carpentry station
repair.design: Low timber bench at left with one secured wood offcut, iron gouge with wooden handle and small wooden mallet. Two simple pegged supports, unobstructed deck at right. Carpenter B: olive waistcoat, cream shirt, brown breeches.

tools.scope: Tools recovered from Queen Anne's Revenge; explanatory object studies
tools.design: Neutral parchment surface. Single named tool at left, period materials and mechanism, no modern grip. Precise object form must follow the linked archaeological reference before production.

rope.scope: Queen Anne's Revenge, early 1718; illustrative rigging work
rope.design: Close working section of timber deck with one hemp rope passing through a wooden block at left, plain canvas furled beyond; no tangled web of unsupported lines. Sailor A returns when specified.

rail.scope: Queen Anne's Revenge, early 1718; illustrative sounding station
rail.design: Timber rail left, sea below, large lead sounding weight attached securely to a hemp line, weight outside hull when lowered. Level open deck right; no depth measurement numbers painted.

chart.scope: Queen Anne's Revenge, early 1718; illustrative navigation table
chart.design: Plain timber table on left with an unlettered parchment chart and metal dividers. One modest lantern only when explicitly requested, never near loose powder. No sextant, GPS or modern compass rose.

medical.scope: Queen Anne's Revenge, early 1718; reconstruction of medical equipment
medical.design: Plain small wooden chest left on table, brass mortar and pestle, folded linen. No modern labelled bottles, skeleton ornaments, blood or identifiable patient. No claim this is the specific captured Charleston chest.

coercion.scope: La Concorde and its capture, 1717; historical explanation
coercion.design: Sober partial view of a wooden ship passage with two clothed adults standing separately and a closed hatch. Restrained lighting, no bondage spectacle, exotic costume or laughing captors. Human dignity; no invented portraits.

paper.scope: Modern explanation of paper recovered from Queen Anne's Revenge
paper.design: Neutral parchment field with a small irregular cream paper fragment and a plain closed early eighteenth-century bound volume. No painted type; local overlays identify the source. Never depict a specific pirate reading this volume as established fact.

comparison.design: Different schematic wooden deck at twilight, one covered candle lantern on left, no inherited QAR landmark or crew portrait. Simplified reconstruction of a reported rule, not a witnessed evening.

diagram.scope: Modern explanatory diagram about early eighteenth-century shipboard life
diagram.design: Parchment canvas with locally drawn simple objects, arrows and labels. No fake archival pages or quantitative chart without data.

research: Anchor: Queen Anne's Revenge in early 1718, with an explicitly imagined workday. One dated comparison concerns Roberts's different crew, 1719–1722, as described in 1724. The script follows practical needs, then changes the viewer's expectation of freedom by naming a forcibly retained cook. Archaeology is not a daily diary: food bones can predate capture, a medicine tool cannot certify a cure, printed scraps cannot identify a reader. Rejected: a precise daily menu, a definite sail needle from the disputed silver object, pirate democracies as universally egalitarian, universal bedtime rules, book-club scenes, burying treasure, walking planks, and detailed vessel geometry unsupported by a plan. Johnson is cited under its published author's name; attribution to Daniel Defoe is disputed. Visual artifact references must be inspected before exact object drawing, but all narrative claims above use passages already read.
description: A pirate ship still needed meals, repairs, navigation and medical care. Step aboard an illustrated reconstruction of Blackbeard’s Queen Anne’s Revenge and follow the work between raids, using objects recovered from the wreck and contemporary accounts. Then meet a cook who did not choose to join—and a book surviving where you would least expect it.
pinned_comment: Which surprised you more: the ship’s practical tools, the forced cook, or the surviving book fragments?

shorts.title: A Pirate Cook Who Never Volunteered
shorts.description: Georges Bardeau was forcibly retained when pirates captured La Concorde. His story complicates the idea that everyone aboard chose pirate life.

shorts.title: A Pirate Ship’s Book Survived in a Cannon
shorts.description: Conservators identified tiny fragments from Queen Anne’s Revenge as pages of Edward Cooke’s 1712 voyage narrative. That does not tell us who read it.

shorts.title: Did Pirates Have a Bedtime?
shorts.description: A 1724 account gives Roberts’s crew an eight o’clock lights-out rule—with drinking allowed on deck. It was not a rule for every pirate.

chapters.title: Your glamorous new assignment
scenes: You have the hat. You have the ship. Unfortunately, somebody has noticed that you also have two perfectly usable hands.
No crew. One secured rope coil and mast base left, continuous deck right.
Welcome aboard. There is no raid happening today, so you can finally enjoy the peaceful life of a pirate.
Same deck with rope and a small wood offcut beside rail. No locals.
First, there is work to do. Then some more work. Your dramatic introduction may have raised the wrong expectations.
Carpenter B works one secured offcut with mallet and gouge; open deck right.
We're using Blackbeard's flagship, Queen Anne's Revenge, as our starting point, off the southeastern coast of North America in seventeen-eighteen.
Sailor A checks a secured rope at left; calm overcast sea, no land or attack.
Three questions, then. What did they eat? Who kept the ship working? And did pirates have a bedtime? Keep that last one.
Three simple locally drawn objects: bowl, mallet and chart.
Our day aboard is imagined. The tools and accounts are real; nobody left a timetable for this particular morning.
Single wood-handled iron gouge on parchment, no person or fake writing.
A shipwreck can reveal what people used without telling you who had the most annoying shift.
Recovered gouge and plain wood offcut at left on the neutral field; right third calm.
It can also spoil a surprisingly cosy picture of pirate life. Not everybody on this ship chose to be here.
Quiet deck, simple closed hatch left, no visible captives or threatening crew.
We'll meet one of those people. First, your enormous appetite has arrived before your first impressive act of seamanship.
Contained cooking hearth and firmly supported pot at left; cook stands behind it, open floor right.
Being between raids does not mean skipping meals. Someone still needs to supply the pot and prepare its contents.
Cook lifts plain wooden spoon from supported pot with plausible grip; no floating lid.
So put the treasure fantasy aside for a moment. Begin with a clue that looks considerably less attractive on a postcard.
One simplified butchered cattle bone on neutral parchment, no blood or person.
For our purposes, an extremely useful bone. What can it actually tell us about dinner?
Same single bone shown larger at left, clean outlined reconstruction; right third calm.

chapters.title: What reaches the pot
scenes: The wreck has produced butchered cattle and pig bones. Meat provisions were part of this ship's story, however unglamorous the leftovers.
Two distinct simplified cattle and pig bone fragments side by side, no meat feast.
Butchered animal bones • Queen Anne's Revenge wreck, 1718
You might picture Blackbeard eating an enormous roast. That is several enthusiastic steps beyond what these bones prove.
One small bone beside a modest empty bowl at left; right third calm, no feast or people.
They give us neither the recipe nor everybody's portion. Today's pot belongs to our reconstruction.
Plain covered pot on established contained hearth, no visible ingredients or people.
Some provisions could predate the pirates' capture. The ship had a previous life, and its rubbish remembers that.
Two-part timeline: La Concorde then Queen Anne’s Revenge; bone symbol straddles boundary.
For the moment, keep the simpler conclusion: people aboard needed supplies, preparation and equipment. The food did not arrive already narrated.
Cook stands beside barrel and supported pot; one plain bowl on side shelf, no restaurant props.
Our cooking space keeps the pot supported and the fire contained. It is a reconstruction, not a recovered galley plan.
Close view of supported pot and brick-lined hearth only; no rope, loose sailcloth or person.
Your contribution today is mostly staring hopefully at the bowl. A valuable skill, although perhaps not enough to earn promotion.
Plain bowl left on shelf, cook absent, clear deck right.
The evidence keeps pointing towards practical work and the people needed to do it.
Single gouge with mallet beside it on neutral field, no other tools.
There was even a named cook caught up in this ship's capture. We will return to how he ended up aboard.
Two clothed adults stand apart in quiet passage, sober expressions; no restraints or weapons.
Imagine having to prepare those meals while the people waiting for them include men who took your ship.
Cook at far left beside secured pot, no cheerful audience; open right foreground.
And once the bowl is empty, the ship remains inconveniently made of things that need looking after while you use them.
Sailor A checks rope at left near mast; no damaged ship or implausible clutter.
Your next stop is the carpenter. Pirate artifacts include rather more than weapons.
Carpenter B stands behind established bench, one mallet and gouge laid safely on it.

chapters.title: The floating workplace
scenes: The recovered iron gouge has a flattened head made for hammering: a small object with a physical working life.
Iron gouge shown with flattened struck head clearly visible, period handle reconstruction distinguished in caption.
Iron gouge • Queen Anne's Revenge wreck, 1718
Tools like this worked wood. We can reconstruct their use, but cannot name the hands that held them.
Carpenter B safely holds gouge against secured offcut with mallet raised slightly; exact two hands visible.
You were hoping for a sword. Instead, someone appears to be offering you a practical skill and a piece of timber.
Tools rest safely on the left bench, carpenter absent; clear deck floor at right.
The tool collection points to carpentry, sailmaking, rigging and navigation. Keeping a vessel useful required different kinds of knowledge.
Four separate locally drawn symbols: carpentry gouge, stitched sail patch, rope through wooden block, and chart dividers. No equipment misidentified.
A raid could bring supplies aboard. It would not turn every passenger into somebody who could repair things.
Sailor A handles a secured coil at left, another adult stands back observing; no battle.
A tool also needs someone who understands it. Your excellent hat has so far failed to supply that knowledge.
Same wood-handled gouge and mallet at left on the neutral field; right third calm.
Some finds remain ambiguous. A large silver needle has competing interpretations; it cannot simply prove sail repairs.
Simplified large silver needle on neutral field, no thread passing through sailcloth and no asserted use.
Large silver needle • debated use • QAR wreck, 1718
On deck, rope and canvas belong to the same practical story. The glamorous ship still depends on unglamorous handling and upkeep.
Sailor A checks one hemp line through wooden block, canvas furled safely behind.
Your hat contributes little here. It does announce a surprisingly theatrical understanding of the job.
One block and secured line at left, no locals, calm open foreground right.
Now imagine being responsible for one of those repairs. Suddenly, a small detail deserves a great deal of attention.
Carpenter B examines secured offcut near tool edge at left; clear right.
But an expertly repaired ship can still be in the wrong place. Keeping it afloat also involves knowing what is underneath it.
Sailor A stands safely inside rail left holding sounding line; weight above water outside hull.
This next piece of equipment is not especially elegant. That is unlikely to bother you when the bottom starts getting closer.
Large elongated lead sounding weight with attachment hole, no painted inscription, neutral field.

chapters.title: Finding water deep enough
scenes: A recovered lead weight, attached to a line, helped find the water's depth.
Sailor A lowers attached sounding weight outside rail; rope travels continuously from hands to weight.
It also helped identify the bottom's character. More useful information than whether the sea looked attractive.
Cutaway sea with weighted vertical line and a clearly labelled seabed; no numeric scale.
Picture our sailor lowering the line. Nothing explodes. No treasure appears. Useful information is arriving in a rather less dramatic form.
Same sailor securely holds line while weight is below frame over side; calm water, plausible stance.
The weight proves this kind of work, not the depth beneath our imagined scene.
Large sounding weight alone on parchment, no ruler or unsupported depth value.
Nor does owning the right tool guarantee a safe journey. Equipment is not a magical promise that people never make mistakes.
Line neatly secured at rail, no locals, open deck at right.
Another small find takes us from the water beside the ship to the problem of working with a chart.
Blank illustrative chart at left on table, metal dividers beside it, no person.
Recovered dividers link the wreck to chart navigation: another small tool with a useful job.
Period dividers partly open over unlettered chart; no hand, numerical scale or modern drawing compass.
You lean over the chart. Understanding what to do with it seems harder than simply looking thoughtful beside it.
Unlettered chart at left, open right third for a separately composited close-up.
Between the rope and the chart, your adventurous home begins to resemble a demanding workplace.
Established deck with sailor A at rope and carpenter B by bench far left; clear right.
You may be between attacks, but the sea has not agreed to stop being the sea until you feel more enthusiastic.
Calm but visibly rippled water left of rail; no people or storm.
Then there is illness. It rarely arrives at a convenient point in anybody's plans.
Plain chest, folded linen and mortar on table left; no patient, blood or labels.
A medicine chest could matter enough to become the object of a serious demand.
Open chest prominently left; mortar beside it, no gold coins.

chapters.title: The chest they actually wanted
scenes: In a published account from seventeen-twenty-four, Blackbeard holds ships and prisoners at Charleston and demands a chest of medicines from the authorities.
Illustrative chest on table with folded linen, no specific original artifact claimed.
The account describes compliance and the prisoners' release. Medicine belongs here to a story of coercion, not charming shopping.
Three sober panels: detained ships, medicine chest, release arrow; no threatened violence shown.
The surviving wreck also contains medical equipment. A brass mortar and pestle belongs to the practical business of preparing substances for treatment.
Brass mortar and matching pestle resting separately with plausible scale, no branded bottles.
Brass mortar and pestle • QAR wreck, 1718
It is tempting to announce that this very tool came from that famous chest.
Brass mortar beside the open plain chest at left; no provenance label; right third calm.
But the connection is uncertain. The tool and the demand survive in different kinds of evidence.
Same brass mortar and pestle on neutral table area, no handwritten receipt or person.
Possessing equipment did not mean someone could cure your illness. A treatment kit cannot prove successful treatment.
Closed chest and folded linen at left, no person in background.
For our imaginary newcomer, that is worrying. Adventure is less enjoyable when you feel terrible.
Established deck in subdued light, rope coil and mast base at left; open deck right.
The object story keeps widening: food, repairs, navigation, treatment. These people had bodies and practical needs, however frightening their reputation.
Four locally drawn icons: bowl, gouge, sounding line, mortar.
Practical needs did not make piracy harmless. Useful people, like useful supplies, could be taken by force.
Sober established deck, two adults working separately left, no celebratory loot.
Which brings us back to the cook. He had a different reason for being aboard.
Quiet passage with one adult in plain cream shirt standing left, sober expression.
His name survives. His story gives this supposed escape from ordinary employment a less comfortable edge.
Same illustrative adult in cream shirt, no portrait claim or invented personal objects.
You can take your hat off when the game stops being fun. He did not have that simple choice.
Empty deck, subdued daylight, no comedy prop or threatening figure.

chapters.title: The cook who did not volunteer
scenes: Georges Bardeau was the second cook aboard the French ship La Concorde. When pirates captured her, they forcibly kept him.
Illustrative clothed cook stands left in ship passage; respectful sober expression, no restraints spectacle.
The vessel became Queen Anne's Revenge. Before that, she had carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic as part of the slave trade.
Sober map-like Atlantic arc with two ship-name labels, no people represented as goods.
So this ship's history includes people whose movement was controlled by others. A pirate flag does not turn that into freedom.
Two clothed adults of different backgrounds stand separately in passage, no smiling captors or pirate flags.
His skill made him useful. We know he was forcibly retained, not every meal he later prepared.
Close view of the supported pot and one plain bowl in the empty cooking space; no actor asserted as Bardeau's likeness.
Continued cooking is plausible. It remains an inference, not a surviving diary of his day.
Supported pot on the contained hearth at left, cook absent; right third calm.
That changes our opening question. What pirates did between raids also depended on who you were and how you ended up aboard.
Sailor A working at rope left, second sober adult observing; no obvious class costumes.
Somebody else's adventure could be your captivity. That belongs in the picture alongside the tools, the meals and the famous captain.
Wider view of the same calm passage: two separated adults and the closed hatch beyond; individual faces, no captivity spectacle.
You can joke about drawing the boring assignment. Actual people aboard did not all share that harmless imaginary situation.
Empty deck with neatly secured rope left, no locals.
There is another easy mistake: imagining that every pirate crew operated under one grand set of rules, like a travelling organisation.
Established deck, sailor A and a second adult working apart at left; open deck right.
The sources contain examples of rules, but an example from another captain cannot quietly become Blackbeard's instruction sheet.
QAR label and Roberts label separated, with explicit later-date band.
For one comparison, leave this ship and consider Bartholomew Roberts's crew, a little later.
Different schematic deck at dusk with a covered candle lantern left; no QAR mast layout.
Their reported rules contain something familiar to anyone told to take the noise outside.
Covered lantern at left on the quiet separate deck; right third calm, no locals.

chapters.title: Did pirates have a bedtime?
scenes: Did pirates have a bedtime? One account gives Bartholomew Roberts's crew a rule requiring lights and candles out at eight.
One covered candle lantern with wick just extinguished on separate Roberts deck; dark sea beyond, no modern clock.
Anyone still inclined to drink afterward was supposed to do it on the open deck. Your evening came with conditions.
Two adults in plain shirts sit separately on open deck left with modest plain cups, no rowdy spectacle.
The same account bans gambling at cards or dice for money. A pirate reputation did not automatically mean an absence of rules.
Simple blank card and dice icons with a crossed-out coin beside them; no readable playing card faces.
REPORTED RULE: NO GAMBLING FOR MONEY
A written rule reveals what someone wanted. It does not prove everyone obeyed it.
Close view of the unlit covered lantern and one empty plain cup on the deck boards; dark sea beyond.
The account even says Roberts's own efforts to curb the drinking failed. Regulation and behaviour are different evidence.
Unlit covered lantern and one empty cup at left; dark sea, no invented disobedience shown.
These articles belong to Roberts's crew, in a book published in seventeen-twenty-four. They are evidence about that crew's intended rules.
Same deck at dusk; one unlit covered lantern, no local people.
The rule tells us where late drinking was supposed to happen. It does not tell us how peacefully every evening ended.
Open separate deck at dusk, two adults in plain shirts seated apart with modest cups at left, lantern unlit; dark sea.
Back aboard Queen Anne's Revenge, we still have one clue to examine. This one survived somewhere you might not expect.
Original mast base and rope coil restored in daylight, not Roberts deck.
For conservators, it became a delicate puzzle: scraps of paper that might still connect this wreck with a printed book.
Tiny irregular paper fragment on neutral field, visibly small relative to closed plain book behind.
No, we have not discovered Blackbeard's personal reading chair. There is one last clue to handle carefully.
Small paper fragment beside the closed plain volume at left; right third calm, no chair or reader.
What would you expect a scrap from a pirate ship to contain? This one points beyond our little working deck.
Small fragment and blank closed bound volume on the neutral field, no chair or identifiable reader.
The tiny fragment survived. Now the challenge was identifying what the printed words belonged to.
Same fragment prominent at left; calm right third.

chapters.title: A book where you least expect it
scenes: Paper survived inside a cannon chamber from Queen Anne's Revenge. Conservators found sixteen tiny fragments and set about identifying them.
Cannon chamber schematic leads to paper fragments panel; exact count label composited locally.
Some printed words were still readable. Researchers identified them as part of a seventeen-twelve edition of a voyage narrative by Edward Cooke.
Small fragment beside blank closed book, no simulated original text.
It was an account of travel around the world. A book about voyages had itself ended up aboard this very eventful ship.
Locally typeset shortened book identification and simple globe icon, no fictional route line.
We cannot name its reader or establish a cosy book club from those surviving scraps.
Fragment alone enlarged on parchment, no reader or reading group.
The discovery is remarkable without that extra story. Printed material was aboard, and its tiny remains survived where paper rarely does.
Two labelled elements: a small paper fragment and a wave line, with the words that paper rarely survives underwater; no fake archival page.
A real object can open a window onto life aboard without supplying every scene beyond it.
Single paper fragment at left on the neutral field; right third calm.
And this clue brings us back to the question. Between raids, life aboard involved far more than waiting beside a treasure chest.
Established working deck, sailor A by rope left, carpenter B at bench further left.
The ship needed food, maintenance, navigation and treatment. Its objects preserve evidence of that work, alongside much harder stories about force.
Four practical icons: bowl, gouge, sounding line, mortar. Sober caption below states that not all aboard chose their work.
Our workday was invented. Its foundation came from tools, remains and accounts, rather than a costume box.
Gouge, sounding weight and mortar clearly separated on parchment, three objects only.
That is what makes the quieter hours worth exploring. They tell you how the famous ship could function at all.
Sailor A checks secured line left; no battle, treasure or sunset spectacle.
You can keep the hat. It has survived the episode admirably. The expectation of a permanent holiday has had a rougher voyage.
Empty established deck, calm slate sea, rope coil left.
Would you rather cook, repair or navigate? Tell us below, then choose your next Life, Previously voyage on screen.
Three clear choice icons: supported pot, gouge, chart; right third left open for the end-screen element placed later.

pronunciations.rule: Listen to every named occurrence and all negatives; no text-only pass.

sound_plan.music: Existing channel theme, low under voice; no triumphant swell over slavery or coercion.
sound_plan.mix: Near -14 LUFS, true peak <= -1 dBTP. Effects below narration at their exact cue. Use silence across reflective pauses.

new_assets.prompt: Quiet gentle seawater moving against a timber hull, slow and even. No gull loop, voices, motor or surf crash.
Brief restrained hemp rope moving through a wooden block, one short pull. No modern winch or metal.
Two light wooden mallet taps on a secured woodworking tool, close and dry. No metal factory ringing.
A wooden spoon stirring a supported iron cooking pot, soft scrape, no loud bubbling.
A small contained cooking fire crackling quietly in a brick-lined hearth. No roaring bonfire or wind.
A heavy lead weight dropping into calm seawater with one modest splash and a line paying out briefly. No scream or crash.
A slow wooden hull creak inside a ship passage, quiet and restrained, one or two creaks. No chains, voices or footsteps.
Calm night water lapping gently against a wooden hull, very quiet. No wind howl or music.
A candle wick pinched out with a faint hiss and a tiny puff, close. No modern click.
